transcript.content: Hello, thank you for coming in. What brings you here today?

Well… the main reason is the voices. I know that sounds abrupt, but it’s been happening enough that I can’t just explain it away anymore. I hear them in my apartment, very clearly sometimes, like women whispering from behind the walls. Not vague noises—more like actual voices, low and close, as if they’re just on the other side of the plaster.

And it’s not only at home. Sometimes when I’m in quiet museum rooms, especially empty ones, I hear them there too. They’ll be whispering about photographs, telling me which ones belong in the archive, like they have some kind of authority over what should be kept and what shouldn’t. It’s very specific, which is part of what’s upsetting. If it were just creaks or people in the hallway, I’d be embarrassed but I could shrug it off. But this feels… directed at me, like I’m supposed to listen and do something with what they’re saying.
Have you ever felt that these voices know things about you that no one else could, or that they're part of some larger plan or system that only you understand?

Yes. I mean… yes, that’s exactly what makes it so hard to talk about without sounding like I’m making some enormous accusation, but I don’t think it’s random.

I’m convinced the museum board and the city arts people have been monitoring my phone. Not in some vague way—more like they’re listening, or tracking who I call, what I’ve photographed, what I’ve been trying to put together. Because the Caribbean archive I’ve been working on, it changes things. It changes how the galleries tell the truth, what gets displayed, what gets buried, whose history is treated as serious and whose is treated like decoration.

And they know that. That’s the part people don’t understand. They act polite, they use all that institutional language, but I can feel that they know what I have. The voices fit into that, like they’re connected to the same system, the same pressure around what belongs in the archive and what doesn’t.

And no one has shown me anything that proves otherwise. People just say, “Why would they do that?” or “That sounds unlikely,” but that isn’t proof. That’s just them not wanting to look at it.
Do you feel that your work or your discoveries are uniquely important in a way that sets you apart from others, or that you have a special role that no one else can fulfill?

Yes… I do. I know how that sounds, and I’m aware people hear “chosen” and immediately decide you’ve gone too far, but there are days when that is exactly how it feels. Like I wake up and there’s this brightness in me, this sense that I’ve been put in the right place at the right time, that all the pieces I’ve been gathering aren’t accidental. I feel radiant, almost like I’m carrying a charge, and the work feels not just important but necessary—like if I don’t do it, no one else will, or they’ll do it wrong, or they’ll let it disappear.

And when I’m in that state, I can see the whole plan so clearly. The archive, the photographs, the connections, the way it all has to be arranged so people finally understand what’s been hidden. It feels bigger than ordinary work. It feels like a responsibility that landed on me because I can see it and other people either can’t or won’t.

But then if someone questions me—if they say, “Maybe slow down,” or “Are you sure this is realistic?” or they start picking apart the plan like it’s just some little hobby—I get furious. Not mildly irritated, I mean genuinely furious. It feels like they’re not just disagreeing with me, they’re trying to erase me. Like they’re trying to wipe out the role I have, or make me small, or make the work disappear before it can exist properly. And I know that reaction is intense, but in the moment it feels completely justified, because it feels like everything important is being threatened.

Have there been times when you felt your mood was extremely high, you needed less sleep, or you felt like your thoughts were racing faster than usual—like your mind was moving too fast to keep up with?

Yes… yes, I do get periods like that, although it’s hard to separate it neatly into “mood” the way people say it. It’s more like I become lit up from the inside. Radiant is the word I keep coming back to, because it feels almost physical, like I’ve been chosen for something and everything suddenly has meaning and direction.

When that happens, my plan feels completely clear to me. I can see what needs to be done, what order it should happen in, why it matters, why waiting would be dangerous or stupid. And if someone says, “Maybe slow down,” or “Are you sure?” it doesn’t feel like a normal disagreement. It feels like they’re trying to stop the whole thing from existing. Like they’re trying to erase me, or make me smaller, or take away the one role I’m supposed to have.

And then I can become furious. Really furious. I know from the outside it probably looks disproportionate, but in the moment it feels like they are interfering with something vital. It’s not just irritation. It’s like this sudden heat, this certainty that they don’t understand and that their doubt is part of the reason everything important gets buried.
Have there been times when you felt down, hopeless, or lost interest in things you usually care about, even your work on the archive?

Yes… there are stretches like that. Long stretches, actually. It’s strange because people assume I’m always in that charged-up state about the archive, always working, always connecting things, but that’s not true.

Sometimes I just sit at my kitchen table for hours, and the little herb pots by the window start drying out because I can’t even make myself water them. I’ll notice the basil going brown, or the rosemary looking brittle, and I think, I should do something, it’s right there, it would take thirty seconds, and then I just… don’t. I sit there.

And I don’t call people back. Friends leave messages, or someone invites me to a concert or a gallery opening—things I normally would care about, things that should feel alive to me—and I can barely feel anything about it. Not even proper sadness sometimes, more like everything is far away and muted. Even the archive can feel like it’s behind glass. I know it matters, I know it matters intellectually, but I can’t always reach the feeling of it.

Have there ever been a time when things felt so overwhelming that you couldn’t function normally for a period of days or longer—like you had to stop working entirely, or someone had to step in to help you manage basic tasks?

Yes. More than once, and I hate admitting that because it makes me sound… incapable, I suppose. But yes, there have been periods where I really could not keep things going in any normal way.

I’ve missed board meetings—important ones—not because I didn’t care, but because I either couldn’t organize myself enough to get there or I was in such a state that it wouldn’t have been safe or appropriate for me to be in public representing anything. And bills would just sit there. Envelopes on the table, notices I knew I should open, appointments written down somewhere and then lost under piles of papers. It became this whole tangle I couldn’t manage.

And I’ve lost people’s trust because of it. Colleagues who used to rely on me started speaking to me differently, like they were bracing themselves for me to forget something or make a scene or disappear. That hurts. It really hurts, because I wasn’t trying to be irresponsible.

My cousin has had to step in—actually sit with me and go through practical things, money things, appointments, what needed to be paid, what had been missed. And a museum administrator had to help manage situations around public events because I wasn’t handling them safely on my own. That was humiliating in a very particular way, because those spaces matter to me, and to need someone else there almost as a guardrail… yes. So yes, there have definitely been times when I couldn’t function normally.
Have there been times when you felt so down or hopeless that you thought about death or wished you were dead?

I… I’m not sure how to answer that in the way you mean. The low periods can feel very bleak, like everything has gone flat and unreachable, but when you ask specifically about death or wishing I were dead, I don’t have a clear, simple example I can hand you.

It’s more that I get swallowed up by the hopelessness, if that makes sense. I can sit there feeling like I’ve become useless, like I’ve failed at things I was supposed to protect or complete. But I don’t know if that’s the same as what you’re asking. I don’t want to overstate it, and I also don’t want to tidy it up just to make it sound better than it is.

So… I suppose my honest answer is that I’m not entirely sure. I know the despair gets heavy. I’m less clear about whether I’ve thought of it in those exact terms.
